title: Big bands and strings versus small groups behind a singer
summary: She prefers a small group to a big orchestra with woodwinds and strings, and talks about how a small group adapts under a singer.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Can I ask this, I mean, just out of interest.
What if, let's say, Benny Carter assemble the band for a performance somewhere, something special like the Newport Festival. (Inaudible -- over talking)
Oh, the songs that I did with Benny?
Yeh.

Oh, yeh, but I would rather do them -- perhaps the band would play the introduction and then fall out and just let me work with the rhythm section and maybe an instrument, and then play the ending as written. I feel that -- I've always felt that arrangements sort of locked you in, you just can't move too much in an arrangement. Of course -- well, that's it.
Okay, that's pretty responsive.

Okay, if you were to record with a large group, would it be more to your taste to have what we normally think of as a big band in jazz or would you incline more to the kind of studio ensemble with lots of strings, woodwinds and so on?
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

I would rather not sing with a big orchestra with all the woodwinds and all the strings. I'll tell you why. Because you're heard on recordings or you're heard on radio or television, you know, with the larger orchestra, and then you wind up working in a club where you got a trio or a whatever and the audience expects to hear what they heard on the recording and it's not the same.

If I may say so, when Sarah Vaughan was making recordings with the big arrangements and violins and this had nothing to do with her rendition or her voice, she would wind up working smaller clubs and believe you me, without the large arrangements, it made a difference. It made no difference in her vocal rendition or her voice --
To me it would have made an improvement.
To me. Yeah. But the audience is funny, you know. They miss that strings and they miss all that big arrangement and I think if you'll notice now --
So you think people came
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
and were disappointed.

Yes. Yes, I'm pretty sure that. For a while it was very difficult to convince the audience that she could sing without all those things, but this had nothing to do with her voice or her renditions, it was just that the audience expected to hear all that big background and it just wasn't there, and I'm pretty sure that now, when Sarah or -- well, you know for certain that when these girls go on their tours that they work with their rhythm section group because they can improvise, they can really stretch out and it's more comfortable that way. With an arrangement you have to stay out of the way of the other instruments or the other part of the arrangement and there is a time in which you may want to improvise around a progression which you hear which isn't written in the arrangement, and you're going to clash.
But with just a small group or trio behind you they can more nimbly adapt themselves to what --
Of course. I'm going
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

to be -- in fact I appear now a lot of times with groups, say six or seven pieces and for the most part I work with the rhythm section with more improvising. For introduction, the piano player plays his four bars and at the end we have some kind of an ending, maybe a (tag line). If I wind up with a group, a larger group, then what I prefer to do if this has to be, just write introductions and endings, that's all, a chord at the end because I feel comfortable that way. I really do. I wasn't as comfortable on that Hoagy Carmichael album as I would like to have been because I felt pretty much locked into that arrangement.
Oh, I'm pretty definite about that.
Also that was your first trip back to the recording studio for a long, long time, wasn't it?

Right. Well, I don't know, they have a difficulty in recording me with a larger group because I have to always wind up in a separate booth because the band overwhelms the vocal and it's not easy for the band to play soft on some

S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC.
WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

passages. How soft can you get to play under the singer. But that's an engineering feat, I mean, nowadays there's different ways you can -- but that is another situation, recording in a studio under proper recording circumstances, always gives me the shakes because it's a cold atmosphere and you really can't do what you want to do then, especially if you're working with a large orchestra. There are no overtones, you know, the studio is usually padded and you don't know whether you're singing in tune or not and you're always wondering, you know, just how it's going to turn out. I know, also -- I'd like for a recording to sound like we were there together. Nowadays they have all kinds of ways that they can put a record together. I've even recorded with earphones, you know, the orchestra was --
In an entirely different place.
Right. And that's not easy either but I like recording easy with a small combination. I think that the recordings that I've

recently for Audiophile and of course the live recordings -- because you're warm and you've got an audience there -- the studio recordings that we did recently, I enjoyed them because there was no pressure, there was no engineering, we just played, you know, and everything was like in one take unless I got a frog in my throat or something like that. One tape and that's it.
You get hung up on these things and then you really get up tight, you can't do anything.
